title: T-K-N
hookLine: tikkun, to fix, to set right

cards: "That which is crooked cannot be made straight." That's Ecclesiastes, Kohelet in Hebrew, sounding tired.
The verb behind made straight is today's root, and he comes back to it: "who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?"
And yet near the end of the same book, the writer is remembered as someone who "set in order many proverbs," and the Hebrew uses the same verb again.
A man who says crooked things can't be straightened spends his days straightening sentences.

teach.h: FOR THE SETTING-RIGHT OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun. Tikkun: fixing, setting right, putting in order.

First, the court. The Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce documents and freeing servants, keeps giving one reason for rules the rabbis put in place: mipnei tikkun ha-olam, for the setting-right of the world.

It's practical. A rule so that a man can't quietly cancel a divorce document he has already sent, behind his wife's back, so that she believes she is free when she isn't. Tikkun olam begins as good order in a courtroom.

teach.h: THE ALEINU: TO SET THE WORLD RIGHT.
teach.b: The Aleinu, said at the end of services, hopes for a day l'taken olam, to set the world right under the sovereignty of the Almighty. Here the fixing is God's, and it's on the horizon. Third, the mystics.
The Kabbalah of Isaac Luria tells of vessels that couldn't hold the divine light and shattered, scattering sparks.
The word for that shattering is shevirah, from yesterday's root; the work of gathering the sparks is tikkun. The break comes first, and the fixing answers it. Fourth, today.
Some Jews use the phrase for social action, mending the world through justice and care.
Others hear the court or the prayer first. All of it lives in these letters. Kohelet may be right that some crooked things stay crooked.
He still set his proverbs in order.

how: Tikkun appears in the Mishnah's court rules made 'for the setting-right of the world', in the Aleinu's hope to set the world right, and in Lurianic Kabbalah's gathering of scattered sparks; some Jews today use tikkun olam for social action.

o: the Hebrew root of fixing, setting right
the Hebrew root of building a house
the Hebrew root of a closing prayer

p: for the setting-right of the world

s: the phrase tikkun olam is only a modern slogan
the Mishnah gives mipnei tikkun ha-olam as a reason for court rules.
in Luria's Kabbalah, the shattering comes before the tikkun
the vessels break, sparks scatter, and tikkun is the work of gathering them.
he uses it for crooked things that can't be made straight, and for setting proverbs in order.

games.q: you're a rabbi of the Mishnah. a man can quietly cancel a divorce document he has sent, behind his wife's back, so she may not know it no longer counts. what do you do?
o: leave it. the law is the law.
put a rule in place to stop it, for the setting-right of the world.
tell her to sort it out herself.
games.why: the Mishnah says Rabban Gamliel the Elder ruled that it not be done, mipnei tikkun ha-olam: tikkun olam as good order in a court.

practice: Walk back through your day and find one small thing left out of order: a reply you owe, a small mistake you noticed and let go, a drawer that won't close. Hold it for a few breaths and decide exactly how you'll set it right.
If you pray, you can hold the Aleinu's hope in mind while you look.

wordCard.voice: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun: tikkun, setting right. And this week's lines in order: ask, answer humbly, free gift, vow, trust, breaking can birth, fix. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: fixing, setting right, from tav, kuf, nun.

carryVoice: Your line: fix. The one crooked thing in front of you is enough for one day. See you tomorrow.
